report.title: The State of AI in the Enterprise: The untapped edge

figures.title: Extent to which organizations use agentic AI, today and expected in two years
figures.subtitle: 3,235 director-level to C-suite leaders across six industries and 24 countries, surveyed August-September 2025
figures.quote: Figure 7: Extent of agentic AI usage (percent) ... Question: To what extent is your organization utilizing agentic AI in its operations?
figures.note: Survey of executives about their own organizations (N=3,235), not an observed count of deployments - an executive saying the company uses agentic AI 'moderately' is a self-assessment with no agreed definition behind it. The 'In two years' series is a stated expectation, i.e. a projection, and expectations of this kind in prior waves of this same survey ran ahead of what materialised. All participating organizations already had at least one working AI implementation in daily use, so the sample is AI-adopting firms rather than firms in general.

figures.title: Share of organizations using physical AI at least minimally, by region, today and expected in two years
figures.subtitle: Director-level to C-suite leaders surveyed August-September 2025, split by Americas, EMEA and Asia Pacific
figures.quote: Figure 10: Extent of physical AI usage (percent) ... Question: To what extent is your organization currently utilizing physical AI (e.g., robotics, automated machinery) in its operations?
figures.note: Self-reported by executives (N=3,235 overall); 'at least minimal use' is a low bar that a single pilot robot would clear, so this is not a measure of robotics intensity. The 'in 2 years' series is a stated expectation, i.e. a projection. Regional bases as printed in the report are 'Americas N=3,235, EMEA N=1,170, AP N=475' - the Americas figure is the full-sample N and appears to be a labelling error in the source, so treat the Americas base as uncertain and the AP base (475) as small.

figures.title: AI benefits organizations say they are achieving today versus benefits they hope to achieve
figures.subtitle: 3,235 director-level to C-suite leaders across six industries and 24 countries, surveyed August-September 2025
figures.quote: Figure 2: AI benefits achieving today vs. hope to achieve (percent) ... Question: With regards to benefits from your AI efforts: Which benefits are you achieving today? Which benefits do you hope to achieve?
figures.note: Executives grading their own organizations (N=3,235); 'achieving today' is a claim, not a measured gain - no revenue, cost or productivity figure is attached to any of it. Multiple-select, so shares do not sum to 100. The two series are answers to two different questions, so a benefit can score lower on 'hope to achieve' simply because respondents already counted it as achieved. An 'Other' category (1% on both series) is omitted here.

figures.title: How deeply organizations say AI has changed their processes and business models
figures.subtitle: Director-level to C-suite leaders across six industries and 24 countries, surveyed August-September 2025
figures.quote: Figure 3: Current approach to transformation with AI ... Question: Which best describes your organization's current approach to process transformation during AI implementation?
figures.note: A single-choice self-assessment: an executive placing their own company in the 'deep transformation' bucket is not evidence that products, processes or business models actually changed. Figures may not sum to 100% because of rounding (34+30+37 = 101). The base printed on this figure is N=3,325, which differs from the N=3,235 printed on every other figure and in the methodology - one of the two is a typo in the source.

points.label: Deep transformation of products, processes, and business models
Little or no change to existing processes

figures.title: How organizations are adjusting talent strategies because of AI
figures.subtitle: 3,235 director-level to C-suite leaders across six industries and 24 countries, surveyed August-September 2025
figures.quote: Figure 4: Talent strategy adjustments due to AI (percent) ... Question: How is your organization adjusting its talent strategies because of the adoption of AI tools/capabilities?
figures.note: Multiple-select self-report (N=3,235); shares do not sum to 100 and a company can appear under several answers. It records what leaders say their organization is doing, not what has been funded, delivered, or reached any worker - the report itself notes that 'fewer than half of companies are making significant adjustments to their talent strategies'. Four options tie at 30%, so their rank order in the source is not meaningful.

points.label: Educating broader workforce to raise overall AI fluency
Designing and implementing upskilling and reskilling strategies
Assessing target talent acquisition levels and hiring specialized talent to drive AI initiatives
Redesigning career paths and career mobility strategies
Assessing changes to the anticipated supply and demand of skills
Providing performance-based incentives for leveraging AI
Combining or reimagining organizations based on new work patterns resulting from AI usage
Changing the balance between full-time, contract and gig workers

figures.title: AI risks organizations say they are most concerned about
figures.subtitle: 3,199 director-level to C-suite leaders across six industries and 24 countries, surveyed August-September 2025
figures.quote: Figure 8: AI risks most concerning (percent) ... Question: Which of the following risks related to AI tools / applications is your organization most concerned about?
figures.note: Stated concern, not incidence: this measures what worries executives, not which risks have materialised or how often. Multiple-select, so shares do not sum to 100. Base for this question is N=3,199, slightly below the 3,235 full sample. Options are fixed choices set by Deloitte, so anything absent from the list cannot register - 'workforce impact' at 30% ranks last among the named risks partly because the list is weighted towards governance and compliance categories.

figures.title: Share of organizations rating themselves highly prepared for broad AI adoption, by domain
figures.subtitle: 3,235 director-level to C-suite leaders across six industries and 24 countries, surveyed August-September 2025
figures.quote: Figure 12: Level of preparedness for AI adoption (percent) ... Question: For each, rate your organization's level of preparedness with respect to broadly adopting AI tools/applications.
figures.note: This is executives grading their own organization's readiness (N=3,235) - a self-assessment with no external benchmark, and the report itself notes strategy and governance scores rise fastest because they 'depend primarily on executive decision-making and policy development' rather than on anything being built. Only the 'highly prepared' share of each four-point scale is shown here; the remaining shares (moderately, slightly, not prepared) are omitted. Deloitte reports year-on-year changes of +4pp technology infrastructure, +3pp strategy, +3pp data management, +6pp risk and governance and +2pp talent, but the arrows accompanying the falls described in the text are not unambiguous in the source, so no change figures are charted here.

figures.title: Types of physical AI expected to have the greatest impact on the respondent's industry
figures.subtitle: 3,235 director-level to C-suite leaders across six industries and 24 countries, surveyed August-September 2025
figures.quote: Figure 11: Types of physical AI expected to have the greatest impact (percent) ... Question: Which area of physical AI do you believe will have the greatest impact on your industry?
figures.note: A single-choice opinion question (N=3,235) about which technology executives believe will matter most in their industry - it is a forecast of belief, not of deployment or investment, and the options were set by Deloitte. Shares sum to 99% because figures may not sum to 100% due to rounding. Because respondents answer for their own industry, the ranking mixes very different sectors into one total.
